title: Memory-Access Costs in Practical AES Attacks
summary: AES attack implementations using larger and smaller memory show about 16-fold and 168-fold speedups, respectively; whether access overhead causes the gap and how to model it remain unresolved.

formal_statement.body: An implementation of the 4-round AES-128 attack, with a reported memory-complexity figure of $2^{24}$, achieved about a $16$-fold speedup over brute force, whereas the preimage attack on 10-round AES-256-DM, with a reported memory-complexity figure of $2^8$, achieved about a $168$-fold speedup. Determine whether the former attack's lower practical speedup is caused by the time required to access its larger memory, and develop a validated method for incorporating memory-access overhead into practical attack-cost estimates.

scope.domain: Practical meet-in-the-middle cryptanalysis of AES-128 and AES-256-DM with memory-aware attack-cost estimation.
parameters: 4-round AES-128 and 10-round AES-256-DM — compared attack targets
16-fold and 168-fold — reported practical speedups over brute force
scope.unresolved_remainder: Determine whether larger-memory access causes the 4-round AES-128 attack's lower speedup and validate a method that incorporates memory-access overhead into practical attack-cost estimates.

progress.summary: The source reports markedly different speedups for the two implementations and tentatively attributes the gap to the cost of accessing larger memory. It provides no controlled validation or hardware-aware cost model.
citation_labels: Boxin Zhao et al., Triangulating Meet-in-the-Middle Attack
